title: Are You a Poor Listener or Just Hard to Influence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece argues that leaders often get mislabeled as poor listeners when the real issue is their unwillingness to change their minds after being persuaded. It draws a sharp line between listening (processing and understanding what others say) and yielding (acting on what was heard). The author contends that frustrated colleagues weaponize the "poor listener" label to pressure independent-minded leaders into compliance, when the honest critique is closed-mindedness or stubbornness, not inattentiveness. It also acknowledges that genuine listening deficits exist, driven by multitasking, distraction, and the cognitive load of formulating a response, and that those skills can be coached. The essay closes by urging leaders to separate the two concepts explicitly when they push back on the "listening" charge.
points: Leaders who resist changing their minds are frequently mislabeled "poor listeners" when the real complaint is that they didn't comply with advice.
There is a meaningful difference between listening to others and yielding to them, and conflating the two lets critics avoid making a better case.
Genuine listening weaknesses do exist, driven by multitasking, distraction, and the mental load of composing a response while someone else is talking.
Leaders should push back on the "poor listener" label by clarifying that they heard and understood the message but remain unpersuaded.
quotes: Although they’re accused of listening poorly, in actuality, they process and comprehend what others say and mean with aplomb.
There is a huge difference between listening to others and yielding to them.
By hurling the label of “poor listener” at them, those frustrated by their recalcitrance hope to put them on the defensive.
There is little doubt that many leaders do indeed find listening to be a significant challenge.
Telling others that you have processed what they have said and understand it but remain unconvinced puts them on notice to make a better case instead of criticizing your listening skills.
